claims.text: The unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy undergoes radiation-induced precipitation under irradiation.
The unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy exhibits negligible irradiation hardening.
Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 has a high density of irradiation-defect sinks.
Adding approximately 0.2 wt.% carbon to W38Ta36Cr15V11 and sintering it will form ultrafine WC.
The ultrafine WC will form a network of particles along grain boundaries.
Sintering at approximately 1200°C under an inert atmosphere permits proper WC-network formation in the carbon-modified alloy.
The WC network acts as a thermodynamic trap for diffusing solute atoms.
Solute capture by the WC network limits the nucleation and growth of radiation-induced precipitates.
The nanocrystalline structure continues to absorb irradiation-induced defects after carbon addition and WC formation.
After irradiation at 500–600°C to approximately 8 dpa, carbon modification will reduce radiation-induced precipitate density by more than 40% relative to the identically processed unmodified alloy.
Carbon modification and WC formation will preserve negligible irradiation hardening at approximately 8 dpa.
WC networks will stabilize grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary stabilization by WC networks will improve the alloy's suitability for practical bulk fabrication.
The proposed precipitation suppression is applicable to energetic-particle irradiation at 500–600°C up to approximately 8 dpa.
Departures from the specified sintering or irradiation temperatures may compromise WC-network formation or effectiveness.
